title: ‘The Dog Stars’ Review: Jacob Elordi’s Sensitive Survivalist Can’t Sustain a Dreary Dystopian Adventure
description: It’s the end of the world as we know it in “The Dog Stars,” and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine? Alive, hanging in ther
body:
It’s the end of the world as we know it in “The Dog Stars,” and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine? Alive, hanging in there, taking it one day at a time. Things could be better, which goes without saying in the aftermath of a flu pandemic that has wiped out most of the planet’s human population, but the four principals here could also be dead, so there’s that. That shrugging, slightly bereft air of just-getting-by is the prevailing mood of Ridley Scott‘s post-apocalyptic survival story, and it’s a tough one to sustain dramatically, much less with any sense of intrepid adventure. Somewhat aptly released at the tail end of a long, loud movie summer, this is a surprisingly low-energy, low-incident blockbuster; you’d appreciate its mellow, character-oriented approach if it gave you any real characters to hold onto.
	

	Peter Heller’s popular 2012 source novel largely did. Concentrated and eventful, it brought Jack London-style terseness and lyricism, as well as some mordant gallows humor, to the oft-solitary saga of Hig, a qualified mechanic eking out a life on an abandoned airstrip in rural Colorado, less than a decade after the fateful plague. (The year in the film is given, most pessimistically, as 2035. Start stockpiling now.) On the page, Hig’s first-person descriptions of his everyday adventures, and of the waning natural world around him, had an honest, melancholy soul to them. That voice doesn’t carry over to the adaptation by screenwriter Mark L. Smith — something of a specialist in survivalist drama, having also scripted “The Revenant” and “The Midnight Sky” — which forgoes narration altogether; the film bets on Jacob Elordi‘s blokey, slightly sad-eyed charm to fill in the gaps.
	

	It’s not a bad bet; it just doesn’t quite pay off. Elordi’s gift as a performer is for mining deeper seams of humanity in unappealing characters, from the douchey trust-fund scion of “Saltburn” to the literal monster of “Frankenstein.” Given a simply dull one, as he is here, he fares less well. The film’s Hig is nice; he’s admirably practical and resourceful; he looks terrific in weathered Carhartt workwear. But even handed the sympathetic accoutrements of a faithful German shepherd sidekick and repeated silent flashbacks to his deceased wife, he remains a bit of a blank. The film’s strangely lackadaisical opening act, heavy on scenes of Hig flying his battered Cessna alone, desperately needs the gruff friction provided by Josh Brolin as Bangley, his fellow survivor turned reluctant platonic life partner.

	Hig and Bangley have an established routine that keeps them alive, if not all that elated to be so. Hig regularly flies to Denver, now a bombed-out ghost town, to pick up supplies from sundry abandoned stores, bars and hospitals. On their compound, they alternate guard duty, on the alert for sporadic bands of intruders, whom Bangley insists be shot on sight. When Hig can’t take it anymore, desperate for any kind of escape, he winds up crash-landing his plane near the spartan farm of grizzled rancher Jack (Guy Pearce) and his lonely daughter Cima (Margaret Qualley), whose routine is similarly, joylessly focused on existence and endurance: The grass, of course, is always greener on the other side of the Rockies. A thin romance ensues. The dramatic tempo stays much the same.

	At its most interesting, “The Dog Stars” mimics the structure and stakes of a classic frontier Western, echoed quite literally in its two liveliest action setpieces: a briefly spectacular yet unperilous buffalo stampede, and a faceoff with a marauding tribe of feral, thickly made-up men on horseback, rather incuriously positioned by the film as an outright enemy force. The old-fashioned cowboys-and-Indians dynamic of this sequence is hard to ignore, as is the shared whiteness of the film’s leading characters: In this dog-eat-dog world, whose brutal survival strategies get to be heroic, and why?

	Smith’s spare, episodic script doesn’t risk such introspection, or indeed much else — save for one whopper of a departure from the novel, late in the proceedings, that sharply wrests the tone from ruggedly earnest wilderness drama to macabre, borderline-camp horror-comedy, only to reverse course so abruptly you wonder if either you or the film dropped out for a quick fever-dream. It certainly yanks your attention amid the generally homey, lolloping rhythm of the film. It also more or less demolishes whatever credibility this future-rustic story world has built up to this point. In this case, Scott’s famously catholic genre interests come at some cost to the integrity of the whole enterprise; you sense he might feel as impatient with these sturdy, morose, faintly drab characters as we do.
	

	All four stars ably play the stoic and sorrowful notes required of them, without finding many secondary or contrasting ones in their dialogue. “The Dog Stars” winds up coasting on their collective capabilities and charisma, as well as on Scott’s autopilot proficiency. If the tirelessly prolific director never seems more than intermittently invested in this material, the strongest passages here thrive on his muscular command of scale, and he can still pick a landscape with the best of them: Northern Italy fills in robustly for the Centennial State here, even though Erik Messerschmidt’s consistently charcoal-washed lensing suggests there’s no magic hour in this unforgiving dystopia. This isn’t a future to be prettified, and fair enough, but that impulse also falls in line with the film’s stubbornly un-fun, eat-your-greens demeanor: Can’t something here thrive rather than survive?

schema.headline: ‘The Dog Stars’ Review: Jacob Elordi’s Sensitive Survivalist Can’t Sustain a Dreary Dystopian Adventure

title: Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson Named 2026 MacGuffin Award Honorees
description:
Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards. 

	The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight
body:
Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards. 

	The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight and elevate the craft of the Property Master by raising awareness, fostering collaboration among craft artisans, educating its members and inspiring future generations of Property Masters. 

	The honorees, recognized for their craftsmanship, service and dedication within the property department and the broader production community in entertainment, were announced Tuesday. 
	

	Castro will receive the Humanitarian Award for his 25-year-long career in the food industry as an executive chef, private chef, culinary instructor and restaurant owner. Over the past decade, he transitioned into food styling for film and television, including “This Is Us,” “Westworld,” “9-1-1,” “Bel-Air,” “Paradise” and “Barbie.” He also founded Imagine Cookin, an in-home cooking class company for neurodivergent individuals.


	Reilly is set to take home the Presidents Award for her career as a food stylist on titles like “Obi-Wan,” “Rebel Moon” and “The Orville,” as well as the culinary creations of “Grotesquerie” and drinkable blood for “American Horror Story.” 

	Wilkinson will be awarded the Lifetime Achievement Award after 40 years in the property department. He served as the property master of “Titanic,” “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom,” “Who Framed Roger Rabbit,” two James Bond films including “GoldenEye” and all eight of the original Harry Potter films. 
	

	“The MacGuffin Awards are about recognizing the people whose creativity, generosity and dedication help define our craft, both on set and beyond it,” said PMG President Jeffrey Johnson. “Luis, Trish and Barry each represent a different and invaluable part of what makes the property community so special. Their careers and contributions reflect the skill, ingenuity and spirit that we are proud to celebrate.”

	The third annual MacGuffin Awards will take place Sept. 12 at the Paramount Theatre in Hollywood. The live ceremony will also reveal winners in categories spanning film, television and commercial work.

schema.headline: Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson Named 2026 MacGuffin Award Honorees

title: Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix’s Action-Noir Series ‘The Shooter’
description: Netflix has confirmed production on “The Shooter” (working title), an action-noir series that pairs Lee Jung-eun with Kim Moo-yul, marking Lee’s fir
body:
Netflix has confirmed production on “The Shooter” (working title), an action-noir series that pairs Lee Jung-eun with Kim Moo-yul, marking Lee’s first outing in an action role.

	Lee’s turn comes on the heels of “My Daughter Is a Zombie,” one of South Korea’s top-grossing films of 2025. Kim joins her fresh off “Teach You a Lesson,” a global hit, and the pair reunite four years after starring together in “Juvenile Justice.”


	Lee Kwon, who directed “A Shop for Killers,” leads the production, working from a script by Kim Hee-su. Studio Dragon produces the series for Netflix.
	

	“The Shooter” follows Jeong Suk-ja, a woman in her seventies whose quiet routine is shattered when her grandson is attacked, forcing her to pick up a firearm for the first time since she was young. Pursuing answers pulls her into the hidden workings of the powerful Chunghwa Group, and into a partnership she never expected, one that upends everything she believed to be true.

	Kim plays Seo Yeon-woo, the strategist behind Jeong’s push for revenge, bringing a sharp eye for judgment and motives all his own.

	Huh Joon-ho (“Notes from the Last Row,” “Mercy for None”) plays Jang Kwang-cheol, who once led the Heukseong Gang and has since risen to chair Chunghwa Group. Choi Sung-eun (“My Name Is Loh Kiwan,” “The Sound of Magic”) plays Shin Ji-hyun, who runs the company’s China office while overseeing Operations Unit 3. Bae Na-ra (“The WonderFools,” “Weak Hero Class 2”) plays Cheon Tae-seok, who assists the chairman while running Operations Unit 2. Seo Hyun-woo (“A Shop for Killers,” “Honour”) plays Yoo Il-koo, the Chunghwa Group outcast who oversees Operations Unit 4. Moon Jong-won rounds out the cast as Um Sang-pil, who runs a bed-and-breakfast and carries a past shrouded in mystery.

schema.headline: Lee Jung-eun, Kim Moo-yul Board Netflix’s Action-Noir Series ‘The Shooter’

title: Can Guy Fieri Unite America? Inside His Lifelong Advocacy of Global Cuisine: ‘When You Talk About Food, You Talk About Culture’
description: “I called Taylor Sheridan to ask him just for some meat for the event. Taylor said, ‘I’ll only give you the meat if I can come cook it.’ And Taylor
body:
“I called Taylor Sheridan to ask him just for some meat for the event. Taylor said, ‘I’ll only give you the meat if I can come cook it.’ And Taylor Sheridan shows up to cook.” 

	Guy Fieri is reminiscing about a 2023 fundraiser he held for Maui fire relief that made $1.7 million for restaurants, service workers and the local Salvation Army. He has endless stories as fascinating as the powerful “Yellowstone” showrunner parachuting in with his ranch’s beef, but he’s always quick to move the spotlight away from himself. 
	

	Although Fieri has an eye-catching appearance, he’d much rather talk about the generosity of friends, the skill of the team that helped to build his Flavortown empire, and the restaurateurs who serve up creative meals on his longstanding Food Network show, “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives.”


	It’s no surprise that when asked to reflect on the show, which has earned him his ninth executive producer Emmy nomination this year, he immediately wants to share the wealth. 

	“It’s recognition of all the hard work of so many people — from the ‘Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives’ locations themselves to my crew,” he says. “Honestly, it’s really about everybody else. That’s the truth of it, and I want them to get the trophy and celebrate the moment after all this time that I think is well deserving of them.” 

	For the uninitiated, “Diners, Drive-ins and Dives” is a travel show with Fieri dropping in on mom-and-pop spots to showcase the special dishes and local color that make these hole-in-the-wall joints unique. 
	

	The team is about to film the 20th season of “Dives,” and Fieri isn’t kidding when he refers to the crew as a family affair, given he’s been with them for so long. For example, Anthony “Chico” Rodriguez has been Fieri’s DP since day one of “Dives”; he still works on every show that Fieri does. 

	“Most everybody has been here 10-plus years,” Fieri says of his team. “The great thing is so many of the players have been cross-trained and have evolved into new positions. I’ve got two or three that were PAs that now operate cameras. They came on as PAs because they wanted a chance to be on the team, and you never know when that break is going to happen.” 

	When it comes to the creative vision of the show, Fieri admits he’s not looking to fix what ain’t broken but rather uses new seasons to nip and tuck the show’s presentation. His first-ever lesson on this came during the early days of the show, which he affectionately calls “Triple-D,” when he had a light bulb moment of how to better profile the business owners. 

	“When I first started ‘Triple-D,’ and I recognized how much voiceover we were doing in the show, I thought, ‘Wait a second. That’s all the stuff that we need to be talking about in current time,’” he says. “From the beginning, when we would do ‘Triple-D,’ I would be in the VO booth for two hours doing a tremendous amount of VO for the show. Now it’s very limited.” 

	More recently, the changes have been to spice up an already successful formula. 

	“We’re not going to change the recipe because people have been coming there to get their chicken pot pie for so many years,” he says. “You don’t want to go and ‘chef it up’ too much. You’re going to stick with what’s been done. But do we play some games? Do we mix things up a little bit? My son Hunter does quite a few with me. I’ve started to bring some other chefs that we know from the network, from ‘Tournament of Champions’ or ‘Guy’s Grocery Games.’ I’ve highlighted some celebrity chef restaurants. So we do little things, but never move off the mark of what is the principle of ‘Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives’, and that is what I call ‘the fabric of the community.’” 
	

	That community aspect has always been the beating heart of the show, one that seems more urgent in 2026 than ever before. “Dives” is one of the biggest series regularly showcasing global cuisine on television screens all over America, as many of the establishments Fieri visits are run by immigrants or first-generation families who focus on traditional preparation and recipes to give others in their community a taste of home, as well as welcoming outsiders. 

	“You know how many people walk up to me and go, ‘Oh, you’re the dude from the diner show. Yeah, the deep-fried pizza, burger, milkshake, monster-fried things.’ And I look at them, and I go, ‘You really must not watch the show that often,’” Fieri says. “If anything, there’s really a tremendous highlight and recognition of ethnicity. That’s one of the things I love about it is we’re a melting pot. The United States is a melting pot. And what better way to show culture than through food?

	“Not everybody likes the same sports. Not everybody likes the same politics. Not everybody likes the same music. But the common denominator of people really is food, if you think about it,” he continues. “That’s one of the pieces that I love: When you talk about food, you talk about culture.” 

	Despite his passion for food, it seems impossible to understand how Fieri is able to keep mustering up his trademark enthusiasm after decades on the job. 

	“Is 20 years a long time? It’s a really long time,” he says, laughing. “But the truth of it is, knowing what it does for my industry … restaurants are my life. I’m a chef that gets a chance to celebrate and highlight his brothers and sisters. It’s the greatest thing. Knowing some of these ‘Triple-D’ locations for as long as I’ve known them, and knowing what it does to their life, it’s overwhelming. I’ll do it as long as the network will have me do it. I’ll do it as long as there’s the need, as long as the fans love it.” 

	When pressed about the future, Fieri speaks about “Dives” as his true calling. 

	“Do I have some sleepless nights? Yeah. Do I put pressure on myself to keep this alive, keep my team employed? These restaurants, they create petitions, they lobby on social media. They write letters. You wouldn’t believe the efforts that people make to get their restaurant, or their favorite spot, on the show,” he says. “The old joke among our crew is, ‘How long are you going to do this?’ I say, ‘You know what? You may see me doing it in a walker.’ It may go that long, because it wouldn’t be in my style to turn off the faucet of opportunity for what it does for these restaurants.” 
	

	And although it’s not the end goal, Fieri wouldn’t mind that Emmy. 

	“I look at things optimistically,” he says. “I look at it and say, ‘Wow, it’s cool to be invited to the big dance.’ Hopefully one of these days, being that we’re the cable network consistently doing it for this many years, maybe this year is their year.”

schema.headline: Can Guy Fieri Unite America? Inside His Lifelong Advocacy of Global Cuisine: ‘When You Talk About Food, You Talk About Culture’

title: Dolly Parton Died After a ‘Brief Battle’ With Cancer, According to Her Reps
description: Dolly Parton‘s reps have revealed her cause of death. The iconic singer died after a “brief battle” with cancer at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center i
body:
Dolly Parton‘s reps have revealed her cause of death. The iconic singer died after a “brief battle” with cancer at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, her reps said Tuesday. 

	“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand,” the statement from her reps to People magazine read.
	

	“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact. After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” the statement said. 


	The beloved country singer, who was 80, had been experiencing dizziness and dehydration the week before when she was unable to make an appearance at her Dollywood theme park. She appeared on video instead to introduce the park’s new Nightflight Expedition roller coaster. A year earlier, she canceled a six-show residency in Las Vegas, saying she was “dealing with some health challenges,” then also canceled the rescheduled dates in May. She explained, “My immune system and my digestive system got all out of whack over the past couple, three years, and they’re working real hard on rebuilding [and] strengthening those, and hopefully I’ll be up to snuff again soon.”
	

	“I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl,” she said just days before she died. Parton’s husband, Carl Dean, died March 3, 2025, at 82.

	Despite her recent health issues, Parton was busy in the past year, making plans for a new Nashville museum and hotel and working on deals to endorse Purina dog treats and launch her Cup of Ambition coffee brand. The musical based on her life, “Dolly, A True Original Musical,” will open on Broadway on Jan. 19, 2027, which would have been her 81st birthday.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton Died After a ‘Brief Battle’ With Cancer, According to Her Reps

title: Shin Mina, Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk, Lee Seyoung’s ‘The Remarried Empress’ Sets November Disney+ Bow
description: Disney+ has set a November premiere date for “The Remarried Empress,” a 10-part Korean drama adapted from the Naver Webtoon series of the same name,
body:
Disney+ has set a November premiere date for “The Remarried Empress,” a 10-part Korean drama adapted from the Naver Webtoon series of the same name, which has drawn nearly three billion views to date.

	The show centers on Empress Navier and Emperor Sovieshu of the Eastern Kingdom, whose marriage unravels after Sovieshu falls for a runaway slave and pursues her affection. Navier agrees to the emperor’s request on the condition that she be permitted to wed a rival monarch, Crown Prince Heinrey of the Western Kingdom, setting off a struggle over love and power that threatens to destabilize the kingdom as Navier works to reclaim her standing.
	

	Shin Mina (“Karma,” “Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha”) stars as Empress Navier, opposite Ju Jihoon (“Light Shop,” “The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call”) as Emperor Sovieshu. Lee Jongsuk (“Big Mouth”) plays Crown Prince Heinrey, and Lee Seyoung (“The Red Sleeve,” “The Crowned Clown”) plays Rashta, the escaped slave at the center of Sovieshu’s pursuit.


	Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol adapted the series for the screen, with Cho Suwon (“Still 17,” “Pinocchio”) directing. The production was shot across multiple locations, including European palaces and other elaborate sets, according to Disney+.

	The series will have its world premiere at the Busan International Film Festival in October, where it is set to screen three of its 10 episodes as part of the festival’s On Screen selection ahead of its full Disney+ rollout.

	“The Remarried Empress” will roll out with a four-episode premiere on Nov. 4, then add two episodes each Wednesday until the series wraps with its finale on Nov. 25.
	

	The series joins a slate of Korean Originals on Disney+ that includes “Made In Korea,” about a Korea CIA agent balancing underworld business dealings with a hunger for power; “Tempest,” centered on a global conspiracy threatening the Korean Peninsula; and “Moving,” which follows South Korean special agents protecting their super-powered children.

schema.headline: Shin Mina, Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk, Lee Seyoung’s ‘The Remarried Empress’ Sets November Disney+ Bow

title: How Modern Appointment Viewing Shows Are Bringing Back ‘Watercooler’ Television
description: There’s nothing better than sitting on the couch to binge your favorite TV show. Or, maybe, there is. In the era of streaming, binge-watching is eas
body:
There’s nothing better than sitting on the couch to binge your favorite TV show. Or, maybe, there is. In the era of streaming, binge-watching is easier than ever. So, it seems potentially incongruous that appointment viewing — watching a television show when it first airs — is so capable of seizing the collective attention of viewers. 

	But fandom is a powerful force, and appointment viewing has tamed the beast into something fearsome. Rather than encouraging viewers to settle in with episode after episode queued up, shows like “Survivor,” “The Pitt” and summer’s guilty pleasure “Love Island” make their fans wait for it. 
	

	It’s not a new concept; “Survivor” has been rocking weekly episode drops since its first foray in 2000 on the Bornean beaches. But it has reached a new fervor with watch parties popping up across the country and “Love Island’”s reality flair convincing millions to watch almost daily as hot singles couple up. 


	There’s obvious incentive to watch when an episode airs if everyone is talking about it; you can hardly open your phone during “Love Island” season without seeing a spoiler. And the reality dating show takes it a step further: Fans can vote live on who must leave the villa and who lives to flirt another day.  

	“Survivor” has dabbled in the fan vote mechanism, too. An extra prize in “Survivor: All-Stars,” casting selection for “Survivor: Cambodia — Second Chance” and gameplay elements in “Survivor 50: In the Hands of the Fans” were all left, well, in the hands of the fans. 
	

	Even a non-reality show like “The Pitt” has capitalized on the power behind scheduled releases. The first two episodes of Season 1 dropped concurrently on Jan. 9, 2025, but every subsequent episode has been released on a weekly schedule. 

	As with any show that received such critical esteem as the Pittsburgh-based medical drama, whose first season won five of its 13 Emmy nominations, Season 2 was accused online of a sophomore slump. Those critical social media fans were accused right back of not watching as intended (i.e., bandwagon binge-ing Season 1 and being upset about starting Season 2 before that was possible). 

	“Survivor” showrunner and Emmy-nominated host Jeff Probst describes the difference between binge-watching and appointment viewing as the difference between a flight and a road trip. Both get you to the destination, but with one, the time spent is part of the experience. 

	Viewers had a week to reckon with the knowledge that there was an active shooter event in the first season of “The Pitt” before the fallout reached the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center in the next episode. Skipping a night of “Love Island” this summer might have meant a fan’s favorite couple exiting the villa — and certainly meant not understanding the social media memes and reactions the next day. Sure, you can binge old seasons of “Survivor,” but you lose the emotional experience of living with Probst snuffing the torch of a beloved player. 

	The time between episodes is where fandom finds its home: reacting, interacting and generally causing a stir around a show in a way that binge-watches can’t always pull off. “The Pitt” has been lauded as a return to classic television, the kind of “water cooler” show that inspires next-day conversations with coworkers. 

	“That waiting period creates a different kind of emotional investment because the audience begins supplying part of the experience,” Probst says. Binge-watching builds momentum, but appointment viewing makes fans sit with the emotion. 

	Physical water coolers may be no more, but modern appointment viewing shows are fighting the impatience of binge watchers, and they’re winning.

schema.headline: How Modern Appointment Viewing Shows Are Bringing Back ‘Watercooler’ Television

title: Universal’s Snoop Dogg Biopic Adds Camron Jones as Tupac Shakur
description: The cast of Universal’s Snoop Dogg biopic is shaping up, with Camron Jones (“P-Valley,” “Panic”) set to play Tupac Shakur, while Lauren London (“Wit
body:
The cast of Universal’s Snoop Dogg biopic is shaping up, with Camron Jones (“P-Valley,” “Panic”) set to play Tupac Shakur, while Lauren London (“Without Remorse,” “ATL”) will portray Snoop’s late mother, Beverly Tate.

	“Outer Banks” alum Jonathan Daviss was previously announced to star as the rap legend in the movie, “Snoop,” directed by Craig Brewer (“Hustle and Flow,” “Dolemite Is My Name,” “Song Sung Blue”). In addition to Daviss, Jones and London, Myles Bullock will also star as Dr. Dre, who discovered Snoop and produced his debut studio album, “Doggystyle,” which reached No. 1 on the Billboard chart in 1993. Tupac and Snoop were labelmates on Death Row Records (you might recall the legendary track “2 of Amerikaz Most Wanted”) and remained close friends until the former’s death in 1996. Tate, also known as Beverly Broadus-Green, is credited with giving her son the childhood nickname “Snoopy,” which later inspired his stage name. She died in 2021 at age 70.
	

	Universal is set to release “Snoop,” described as the “definitive biopic of the entertainment mogul and icon,” on Aug. 6, 2027.


	Snoop Dogg is producing the project, which will incorporate music from his vast catalogue, alongside Imagine Entertainment’s Brian Grazer (“8 Mile”) and Allan Mandelbaum and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker. Brewer directs based on his rewrite of Joe Robert Cole’s (co-writer of both “Black Panther” movies) original script. 

	“Snoop” is the first project under Death Row Pictures’ overall deal with NBCUniversal Entertainment & Studios. Senior VP of production development Ryan Jones and director of development Tony Ducret will oversee the project for the studio. 
	

	Jones is best known for his starring role as Bishop on “Panic,” the young adult drama based on Lauren Oliver’s bestselling novel for Amazon’s Prime Video. Jones, whose filmography also includes roles on “grown-ish,” “The Purge” and “Shameless,” began acting as a child raised in San Ramon, California; he went on to earn a BFA in acting from the University of Southern California, and studied abroad at the British American Drama Academy in Oxford, where his training focused on Shakespeare. Jones will next star as Quan in the highly anticipated third season of Starz’s “P-Valley.” He is represented by Clear Talent Group and Venture Entertainment Partners. 

	London is a Los Angeles native whose career has spanned such projects as Netflix’s “You People,” Amazon’s “Without Remorse,” “ATL” and “Games People Play.” In addition to her acting resume, London is an entrepreneur and activist, focused on mental health awareness. She is represented by WME, FoxRothsChild, Yaneley Arty and 1v1 Entertainment.

	THR first reported Jones’ casting, while Deadline broke London’s involvement.

schema.headline: Universal’s Snoop Dogg Biopic Adds Camron Jones as Tupac Shakur

title: Beyoncé Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘You Were the Barometer’
description: Beyoncé has paid tribute to country icon Dolly Parton, who died on August 25, calling her “the barometer” and thanking her for the impact she had on
body:
Beyoncé has paid tribute to country icon Dolly Parton, who died on August 25, calling her “the barometer” and thanking her for the impact she had on the world.

	In a statement posted to her website, Beyoncé wrote, “Dolly, you were the barometer. The north star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship. I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”
	

	Beyoncé had worked with Parton and recorded a reworked cover of “Jolene” for her 2024 album “Cowboy Carter,” altering the original’s lyrics and song structure. Where Parton begged and pleaded a woman not to steal her man on the original “Jolene,” Beyoncé transformed the tune into a warning shot: “I can easily understand why you’re attracted to my man / But you don’t want this smoke, so shoot your shot for someone else,” she sang.


	Parton had hinted weeks before “Cowboy Carter” that Beyoncé had recorded her own version of “Jolene,” and following the album’s release, Parton took to social media to give the cover a stamp of approval. “Wow, I just heard Jolene,” she wrote on social media. “Beyoncé is giving that girl some trouble and she deserves it!”

	Parton’s participation in “Cowboy Carter” didn’t end there, as she appeared on the album with two cameos. She introduced the song “Tyrant” and had her own “Dolly P” interlude just before “Jolene.” “Hey miss Honey B, it’s Dolly P. You know that hussy with the good hair you sing about?” she said on “Dolly P,” referencing Beyoncé’s 2016 song “Sorry” and the line “Becky with the good hair.” “Reminding me of someone I knew back when, except she has flaming locks of auburn hair, bless her heart. Just a hair of a different color but it hurts just the same.”
	

	She had previously supported Beyoncé recording a country album on social media, shortly after the pop star became the first Black woman to top Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart when “Texas Hold ‘Em” debuted at No. 1. “I’m a big fan of Beyoncé and very excited that she’s done a country album,” she wrote. “So congratulations on your Billboard Hot Country number one single. Can’t wait to hear the full album!”

schema.headline: Beyoncé Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘You Were the Barometer’

title: How the Muppets Were Brought Back to Life for the Disney Special
description: The lights were lit and the music played in the Muppet Theatre once more this year. But before the curtain opened on Kermit the Frog in an episode o
body:
The lights were lit and the music played in the Muppet Theatre once more this year. But before the curtain opened on Kermit the Frog in an episode of television for the first time in 10 years, the show had to be put together — by the humans behind the characters. 

	Simultaneously a nod to the classic “Muppet Show,” which ran from 1976 to 1981, and something entirely new to this era of the beloved characters, “The Muppet Show” special starring Sabrina Carpenter notched six Emmy nominations, including production design (variety special), character voice-over performance for Matt Vogel as Kermit the Frog and writing for a variety special. 
	

	The Muppets have bowed in various formats over the years (films, TV specials and even the World Cup Final halftime show this summer). Putting on a Muppet show is always an elaborate production involving angles, runways, monitors and sets that make the audience forget that these are puppets. “It’s this big magic trick that we’re doing,” Vogel says. 


	That’s where production designer Denise Pizzini steps in. Her first foray into building for the Muppets was a decade ago, when she notched an Emmy nomination for “The Muppets” series. She’s familiar with the insider tricks of building in the Muppet Theatre: how to set up boxes and risers to even out the height of performers and humans, the 36-inch height standard for walkways for guest stars like Carpenter above Muppet performers and their monitors hidden on the ground.  



	

	



	Around this infrastructure, Pizzini and her team reconstructed the original Muppet Theatre, from the iconic arches to the filigree to the safety curtain with the door Kermit pops out of in the opening sequence. “I wanted to get that exactly like it should be, like the original show, because that creates a feeling,” she says. 
	



	

	



	And it paid off. For original Muppet fans, Vogel hopes “it feels, it smells, it looks, it sounds, it acts and it just feels like the original show.” The Muppets as a brand are something uniquely familiar to generations. Part of being a Muppet performer, Vogel says, is paying homage to the soul of the original character and performer (in his case, Muppet creator Jim Henson himself). Part of it is imbuing a little personal flair to create an authentic representation of a modern Kermit. 



	

	



	The familiarity of the characters is something writer Albertina Rizzo kept in mind, too. “You can’t veer from their core being,” she says. Kermit wouldn’t say YOLO; internet vocabulary doesn’t fit with the Muppets. “They exist in a different time and space,” she adds. 

	Rizzo took inspiration from “Saturday Night Live” and variety shows of the 1970s. There’s a sensibility to Muppet comedy that speaks to her background in late-night television, where the revolving door of guests necessitates different styles. A Miss Piggy joke wouldn’t work for Kermit, and vice versa.  

	One thing universal across the Muppets is a certain kind of goofy, physical humor. Muppets never get hurt, Rizzo says, but they certainly can have doors fall on them (as Kermit does in the special) or zoom in and out of frame on out-of-control roller skates (like Gonzo). 

	“Muppets are best when in motion,” Rizzo says. That’s in part due to the delight of a well-done physical gag, but also because she finds the fantasy can lapse if the audience is allowed to look too closely at a Muppet for too long. She kept the jokes tight and the physical bits quick. 

	The collaboration required to make that rapid comedy work brought Rizzo into conversation with Pizzini and puppet captain Bill Barretta. Barretta has been working with the Muppets since 1991. Pizzini credits him as the person she would drag over to set to troubleshoot the physical necessities of the script. 

	The production design team did countless tests to ensure different sets worked properly. Pizzini says she watched the original opening sequence so many times that she had the song stuck in her head. After seeing the setup for a stunt where Gonzo roller skates through fire and swinging blades, she recalls performer Dave Goelz hugging her, ecstatic about the complicated set they pulled off. 
	

	“I’ve always thought that these Muppet performers were just pure artists,” Pizzini says. “There’s a purity about what they do, and they’re so passionate and excited, and they really embrace these characters, and that just spills over into the whole crew.”   

	Goelz is the only Muppet performer still in his original role. For him, it is a true return to the original Muppet Theatre. For Vogel, who has been the full-time Kermit performer since 2017, the special was something he had “dreamed about doing for a long time.” 

	Henson created the Muppets in the 1950s, and he performed as Kermit until his death in 1990. He never wanted the Muppets to be a kids show like “Sesame Street,” although many Muppet performers throughout the years have also worked on “Sesame Street” (Henson and Vogel included).  



	

	



	Rizzo says it was helpful to have several people familiar with an 11:30 p.m. audience in the writers’ room. “We wanted to have jokes where an adult would hear it and get it, and a kid would hear it and laugh at it, but not know why they’re laughing,” she says. With a guest star like Carpenter, whose cheeky lyrics are key to her pop diva brand, the writers were able to embrace what Rizzo calls the “inherent sweet corniness” of the Muppets. 

	The core magic of the Muppets is fiercely protected. Pizzini remembers forgetting Scooter was a puppet during her first Muppet collaboration in 2016. “I love that the performers and Muppet Studios really guard the brand and take good care of them and are very loyal to the original Muppets,” she says. 



	

	



	At the same time, each new iteration of the Muppet Show is a chance to introduce a new generation to the magic of the Muppets. “You’re coming in and you’re discovering these engaging characters that are really funny, that are musical, that are magical, that draw you in that same way,” Vogel says. For him, part of the beauty of the Muppets is that everyone can see a bit of themselves in the characters. 

	Vogel grew up with the original Muppet Show. He created his first puppets in elementary school out of his dad’s old T-shirts and put on shows in his neighborhood. But even then, he never thought he would be a puppeteer. “Let alone go like, ‘I’ll be Big Bird one day’ or ‘I’ll be Kermit one day,’” he says. “I never would have had those thoughts growing up. Even as an adult, I never had those thoughts really until they happened.” 
	

	The next Muppet Show might be one of those dreams that you don’t believe can happen until it does. Disney has not greenlit a full show, though many Muppet fans are hopeful that the special can act as a kind of pilot episode. But for the performers who have worked together for years, even decades, returning to the Muppet Theatre even once was worth it. “When we all got together for that first scene,” Vogel says, “it felt like coming home.”

title: Dolly Parton Cause of Death Revealed
description:
Country Star Dolly Parton
                          Cause of Death Revealed
body:
Country Star Dolly Parton
                          Cause of Death Revealed
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dolly Parton died following a brief battle with cancer ... TMZ has confirmed.
      
    
            Parton’s reps said in a statement to TMZ ... she was surrounded by loved ones at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville when she died.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Her reps say Dolly spent her life bringing "joy, laughter, hope and integrity" to everything she touched, and point to her enormous generosity through Imagination Library and her support of medical research.
      
    
            They add her unconditional love for others was the driving force behind the lasting impact she leaves behind.
      
    
            The icon died Tuesday at 80 ... and the news hit especially hard because, as TMZ reported, her death was sudden even for loved ones who knew she'd been dealing with health issues.
      

            Sources told us Dolly's family and friends knew she was sick ... but still believed she'd pull through, making her death a shock to those closest to her.
      
    
            Dolly had been hospitalized in Nashville for four days before her death after battling a number of health problems in recent months.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Celebrities quickly paid tribute to Dolly ... sharing emotional messages and memories of the legend -- including two of her closest famous friends, Jane Fonda and Reba McEntire.
      
    
            Jane -- Dolly's "9 to 5" costar and longtime friend -- remembered her as funny, generous, and completely one of a kind.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Reba also mourned Dolly ... saying there would "never ever be another" and sharing memories from their decades-long friendship.
      
    
            Of course, Dolly leaves behind one hell of a legacy ... she spent more than 6 decades in showbiz ... becoming one of the biggest names country music has ever produced with classics like "Jolene," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You."
      
    
            And her reach went way beyond music ... Dolly became a movie star, businesswoman, and beloved philanthropist, with her Imagination Library giving books to millions of children.
      
    
            From humble beginnings in Tennessee to country music royalty ... Dolly became a true American icon.
      
    
            She was 80.

            The Hollywood Hills home where D4vd allegedly murdered Celeste Rivas Hernandez is sitting vacant and hoping for a new tenant ... and the rent just went down.
      
    
            According to real estate records, the rental price dropped from $23,950 a month to $21,500 as it sits quietly on the market.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            D4vd moved out in September 2025, just days after police searched the property in connection with the investigation into Celeste's death.
      
    
            Prosecutors allege D4vd invited Celeste over to the home in April 2025 ... and she was never heard from again.
      

            The home was listed for rent in February ... and on Aug. 16 the price dropped over 10%. It's unclear if anyone has lived there since D4vd moved out.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, cops sprayed luminol and tested residue found in the Hollywood home after obtaining a search warrant last year ... finding chainsaws, potential blood stains, and a cut-up inflatable pool -- all items investigators used as evidence during D4vd's preliminary hearing.
      
    
            It's unclear whether the home's connection to the investigation has affected its rental prospects or prompted the price reduction.

title: Dolly Parton's Death Was Sudden, Even For Loved Ones Who Knew She Was Sick
description:
Dolly Parton's Death
                          Came as Sudden Shock to Those Close to Her ...
body:
Dolly Parton's Death
                          Came as Sudden Shock to Those Close to Her ...
                          Despite Known Health Issues
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 25, 2026
                
                            12:52 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 25, 2026
                                4:17 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dolly Parton's death came as a sudden and unexpected shock to those closest to her ... even though people in her inner circle knew she had been sick ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources familiar with the situation tell TMZ ... when loved ones learned Dolly had been hospitalized last week and wasn't doing well, they began rushing to Nashville to be by her side.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told they did not expect she would die during this hospital stay, believing she would recover and be released as she had following past health setbacks.
      

            As we first reported, Dolly died Tuesday morning at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, after she was admitted early Friday with kidney and autoimmune issues.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Dolly had dealt with health complications in recent months, including immune-system and digestive issues, kidney stones, and medication-related problems. She also canceled appearances and postponed her Las Vegas residency while focusing on her health.
      
    
            Still, we're told Dolly's death was unanticipated.
      
    
            Family sources previously told us a small, intimate ceremony is being planned in Nashville in the coming days, with her closest relatives and loved ones expected to gather to celebrate her extraordinary life and legacy.
      
    
            We're told there are no solidified plans for a public funeral or celebration of life just yet ... but it's still early.
